The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven to the coast for a weekend getaway, and I remember standing at the edge of the sand, toes sinking into the damp earth, staring at the endless blue horizon. The waves crashed against the shore in a rhythm that felt like a heartbeat—steady, relentless, alive. I didn’t understand then how something so vast could also feel so intimate, how the same water that stretched beyond sight could cradle my small hands when I finally dared to wade in.

Years later, I still find myself drawn to water. There’s something about its unpredictability—the way it can be calm one moment and furious the next—that mirrors life itself. It teaches patience, resilience, the art of letting go. When I’m stressed, I close my eyes and imagine the sound of waves, the way they erase footprints in the sand as if they were never there.

But water isn’t just a metaphor. It’s a necessity, a lifeline. Without it, we wither. And yet, we take it for granted, waste it, pollute it. Maybe that’s why the ocean fascinates me so much—it’s a reminder of both our insignificance and our power. We are tiny compared to its scale, but our choices shape its fate.

Sometimes, when I’m feeling lost, I think about how the ocean doesn’t resist change. It adapts, flows, finds new paths. Maybe that’s the lesson I’m still learning.
